description: This teaching case examines how Hoshitech Industries, the Thai subsidiary of a Japanese precision manufacturer, handled the 2011 Chao Phraya flood in central Thailand, which lasted more than five months, caused damages and losses estimated at 1.43 trillion baht, about 43.9 billion US dollars in 2025 value, affected more than 16 million people and inundated seven major industrial estates and parks. Hoshitech was among 1,823 affected factories and lost about 950 million baht, some 30 million dollars, through damaged equipment, lost inventory and unfilled orders. The case traces decisions before, during and after the flood: conflicting warning signals, coordination with headquarters in Japan, breaches in flood barriers, weaknesses in business continuity management and plans, recovery and later improvements. It was written by Tadashi Nakasu of Chulalongkorn University and Muthita Kanwerayothin and published by Nikkei BizRuptors on 16 December 2025. Coverage is one factory site. The abstract and contents are free online; the full case needs a login under Nikkei's purchase terms. Caveats: it is based mainly on secondary data for teaching, and copying is not permitted. For simulation it gives a documented decision sequence for modelling how manufacturers respond to slow-onset floods and how supply chains are disrupted, useful in resilience and emergency response studies. It is related to the Resilinc supply chain risk platform record in this catalogue.
